items.title: Generate JSONL_STRUCTURE_AND_FORMATTING.md from real fixtures
items.detail: The session opened by asking Claude to "ultrathink" about docs/JSONL_STRUCTURE_AND_FORMATTING.md, and the result was called "hot garbage" because "at no point did you actually look at the jsonl files in question so you just made stuff up." That is a documentation-drift failure: the doc described the .jsonl format aspirationally rather than from observed samples, so any reader (human or agent) who trusted it was misled. The `thinking` message type, for instance, was absent and had to be discovered live twice (once from a snippet, once from a full sample line). The fix is to make the doc a generated artifact, not hand-maintained prose: derive it from the sample .jsonl files in spec/fixtures, enumerate every message shape actually seen (thinking, isCompactSummary, leafUuid, isMeta, isApiErrorMessage, tool_use/tool_result pairs), and add a test that fails when a fixture contains a top-level key or message `type` the doc does not list. That converts "the doc is stale" from a silent trap into a red test.

items.title: Commit discover_structure as a first-class repo tool
items.detail: The developer unblocked the whole redesign by hand-writing discover_structure.rb and pasting discover_structure.out, then saying "it doesn't seem too complicated and we should just be able to process the entries liniarly." That structure-characterization capability is exactly what the earlier documentation should have been backed by, yet it lived as a throwaway script outside the project. It belongs in the repo as a supported command (e.g. bin/discover or a rake task) that scans a session directory and prints the observed key/type histogram. Because Claude Code's own .jsonl format is an external contract that changes across CLI versions (the fixtures here are version 1.0.72), a committed discovery tool lets a future contributor re-characterize the format in one command and regenerate the docs from item 1, instead of re-encountering the same "made stuff up" failure the next time Anthropic ships a new message type.

items.title: One fixture per message variant plus an iterate-all test
items.detail: Fixtures entered the repo reactively and piecemeal: first "let's copy the current jsonl files into a specs/fixtures directory, so we can use them for testing," then the pathological nested-code-block message was only added as spec/fixtures/backticks-in-backticks.json after it had already corrupted VIBE.html in production, and the `thinking` type similarly only got a fixture after it broke. The repo needs a curated fixtures set holding at least one minimal representative of every known message variant, plus a single spec that runs the full exporter over every file in spec/fixtures/ and asserts it neither raises nor emits malformed markdown. That turns edge-case handling from "user notices breakage, hands over a sample, we patch" into a standing regression net, and gives the two hard-won cases (thinking, unbalanced fences) permanent coverage.

items.title: CI that fails when lib/ changes without spec/ changes
items.detail: The single most repeated friction in the session was the developer policing test discipline by hand: "instead of writing test scripts and deleting them, you can write actual tests," then "always update the tests," then "i didn't see you add or update tests for this." Each was a manual catch of the same structural gap: nothing in the repo makes test updates mandatory, so an RSpec-covered project silently accepts lib changes with no accompanying spec change, and even tolerates throwaway one-off scripts standing in for real specs. A CI workflow (GitHub Actions) that runs `rspec` on every push, plus a check that flags a commit touching lib/ with no corresponding touch under spec/, would make "always update the tests" a property of the pipeline rather than something the user must re-assert every few turns. This is repo tooling, not a prompting habit — the guard should exist whoever is typing.

items.title: Harden the markdown code-block parser with an invariant spec
items.detail: Nested and unbalanced code fences (VIBE.md's "code block that contains backticks") were a genuine structural weak point: ad-hoc regex attempts failed repeatedly, and the working solution, lib/markdown_code_block_parser.rb, had to be sourced externally from Opus and uses heuristics to disambiguate which fences pair. Heuristic parsers rot silently unless pinned by tests that encode the intended behavior. The developer already articulated both the specific expected pairing ("sets 1 and 6 ... sets 2 and 3 ... sets 4 and 5") and, more valuably, a global invariant: "there is an unmatched set of backticks which just appears as simply as ``` (the last one) in the html and that should never happen." Encode that invariant directly — a spec asserting the parser's output over any fixture never leaves a dangling fence in the rendered HTML — alongside example-based cases for the nested scenario. Without it, the next markdown quirk will regress the heuristics with no signal until a preview visibly breaks again.

items.title: Round-trip test between preview timestamps and --from/--to parsing
items.detail: The developer had to ask outright whether the tool's own output was machine-readable by its own inputs: "if i copy 'August 09, 2025 at 06:03:43 PM' from the preview, and give it to the --from paramter, does it work?" That is a real coupling the repo leaves untested — the human-facing timestamp format rendered in the header/preview and the timezone-aware date parser behind --from/--to/--today evolved separately (the header even shipped with newline and timezone bugs), so nothing guarantees they agree. Add a round-trip spec: render a timestamp through the exact preview formatter, feed that string back into the --from parser, and assert it resolves to the original instant in the user's timezone. That closes the loop the developer had to verify by hand and prevents the two sides of the date handling from drifting apart as either format changes.

items.title: Remove the machine-local notify dependency and smoke-test portability
items.detail: The code shelled out to a `notify` helper that only existed on the author's machine: "remove the use of 'notify'. this is a function i have locally, but other users will not have it." That is a portability defect — core behavior depended on an environment-specific shell function, so the tool would fail for anyone else running it fresh. Beyond removing this instance, the repo should gain a minimal smoke test or CI job that runs bin/ccexport end-to-end against a fixture in a clean environment with a bare PATH, which would have surfaced the notify dependency automatically rather than requiring the author to spot it by memory. For a CLI meant to be shared, "runs on a machine that is not the author's" deserves to be an executed check, not an assumption.
